steps.title: Time does the heavy lifting
steps.body: €10,000 earns 5% a year. In year one, that is €500. In year two, the €500 earns interest too. Growth on growth is called [[compound-interest]]. After 30 years, there is about €43,000. Most of it is growth, not money you paid in. Time does the heavy lifting.

steps.prompt: Move the years. When does the growth become bigger than the €10,000 paid in?

goal.hint: At 5% a year, it takes about 15 years for the growth to pass the money paid in.

steps.prompt: €10,000 grows by 5% a year, and each year's growth grows too. How much is there after 18 years?
steps.reveal: About €24,000. Without growth on growth, it would be €19,000. The extra €5,000 is interest earned on interest.

steps.prompt: Anna saves €100 a month from age 25 to 35, then stops. Ben saves €100 a month from 35 to 65. Both earn 7% a year. Who has more at 65?
options: Anna, though she paid in €24,000 less
Ben, because he paid in three times as much
steps.explanation: Anna ends with about €140,000, Ben with about €122,000. Anna's money had 10 more years to grow. With [[compound-interest]], an early start can beat a bigger amount. The 7% is an example, not a promise.

steps.prompt: True or false: with compound interest, money grows by the same amount every year.
steps.explanation: False. Each year, the interest is paid on a bigger amount, so the growth itself grows.

steps.title: Your interest grows too
steps.body: Your savings account holds **{savingsBalance}** at **{savingsRate}** a year. The bank adds the interest to your balance, and next year that interest earns interest too. A long [[time-horizon]] makes the effect bigger.

steps.prompt: Your savings, at your rate. See what time adds on top of your money.

goal.hint: Move a slider to see the result change.

steps.note: The amount and the rate start at your real numbers. This is an example, not a forecast. It does not count rising prices.

scenes.title: Growth on growth
scenes.desc: Each year's interest earns interest too. This is [[compound-interest]]. The longer the money waits, the stronger it gets.

captions.text: €10,000 earns 5% a year. In year one, that is €500.
In year two, the €500 earns interest too.
Growth on growth is called compound interest.

goal.hint: Move the years slider to 15 or more.
